pages.text: Class 3 wanted to visit the regional museum to see old drums, cloth and tools. “Somebody must write to the headmistress,” said the class prefect. Everyone turned to Regina, who was good at English. “Me?” she said. “Fine, I will.” That evening, she wrote a letter in the same friendly way she wrote to her cousin: “Hi Madam, we really want to go to the museum, please let us go, it will be so fun.”

“Somebody must write to the headmistress,” said the class prefect.
Everyone turned to Regina, who was good at English.
“Me?” she said.
“Fine, I will.” That evening, she wrote a letter in the same friendly way she wrote to her cousin: “Hi Madam, we really want to go to the museum, please let us go, it will be so fun.”
pages.alt: A girl writes a casual letter at a desk while classmates hold a poster saying museum trip.

pages.text: Mr Allotey read her draft and raised an eyebrow. “It is warm and honest,” he said. “But this is a letter to the headmistress. It is a formal letter. The reader is important, and she does not know you well. Informal letters are for family and friends. Formal letters are for officials, offices and requests.” Regina looked at her draft. “So I have to start again?” she asked. “You have to dress it for the occasion,” said Mr Allotey.

pages.text: He pinned a chart on the board. “First, your own address at the top right, then the date under it. Below that, on the left, the receiver’s designation and full address: The Headmistress, then the school name, box number and town. Then the salutation: ‘Dear Madam,’. Notice there is no first name. We use ‘Dear Madam’ or ‘Dear Sir’ for an office holder.”

Below that, on the left, the receiver’s designation and full address: The Headmistress, then the school name, box number and town.

Notice there is no first name.

pages.alt: A chart on a board showing a formal letter with the sender address, date and receiver address labelled.

pages.text: “Next comes the subject heading,” said Mr Allotey. “It tells the reader the purpose before she starts. For example: REQUEST FOR PERMISSION TO VISIT THE REGIONAL MUSEUM. Write it in capital letters and underline it.” Regina wrote it down. “And the body?” she asked. “Three small paragraphs,” he said. “Why you are writing, the details with reasons, and what you are asking for. Your language must be polite, clear and persuasive, so that the reader wants to say yes. And no contractions: write ‘do not’, never ‘don’t’.”

Write it in capital letters and underline it.” Regina wrote it down.

“Why you are writing, the details with reasons, and what you are asking for.
Your language must be polite, clear and persuasive, so that the reader wants to say yes.
And no contractions: write ‘do not’, never ‘don’t’.”
pages.alt: A student writes a capitalised subject heading on a page with a ruler underline.

pages.text: Regina began again. “I am writing on behalf of Class 3 to request permission for a one-day educational visit to the regional museum. The visit will link to our Social Studies lessons on culture and history. The visit will help us to understand our heritage, and it will cost parents very little. We propose to travel on a Friday with two teachers, and parents will be informed in writing. We shall be grateful for your kind consideration.” Mr Allotey read it slowly and nodded.

We shall be grateful for your kind consideration.” Mr Allotey read it slowly and nodded.
pages.alt: A girl writes the body of a formal letter as a teacher reads over her shoulder.

pages.text: “Now the closing,” said Mr Allotey. “If you started with ‘Dear Madam’, you end with ‘Yours faithfully’. If you had begun with a name, such as ‘Dear Madam Gyamera’, you would end with ‘Yours sincerely’. Then your signature, and below it your full name and class. No kisses, no ‘Your friend’, no nickname.” Regina giggled. “So it is the opposite of Dear Cousin,” she said. “Exactly,” said Mr Allotey.

No kisses, no ‘Your friend’, no nickname.” Regina giggled.
“So it is the opposite of Dear Cousin,” she said.
“Exactly,” said Mr Allotey.
pages.alt: A girl signs a formal letter with a full name and class below the closing.

pages.text: The headmistress, Madam Gyamera, read the letter and smiled. “A clear, polite request,” she said. “Permission granted, with two conditions: signed parent slips and a short report afterwards.” The class cheered. On the museum trip, Regina stood in front of a drum older than her grandmother. “Dear Cousin, wait until I tell you about this,” she whispered. Then she grinned. “That is the informal letter, for tonight.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: before you write any letter, ask who the reader is and what you want. A friend or relative gets an informal letter: your address, the date, “Dear” and a first name, an introduction, a body, a friendly conclusion and a close such as “Yours ever”. An official gets a formal letter with all eight features: your address, the date, the receiver’s designation and full address, “Dear Sir/Madam”, a heading, “Yours faithfully”, your signature and your full name. Some school materials allow contractions such as “won’t” in informal letters, but a formal letter never does. The end.
